title: Bombay High Court Makes Road Firecracker Ban Year-Round Ahead of Diwali
excerpt: The court extended its September order to all festivals, directing Maharashtra authorities to publicise the public-space ban and set up a complaint mechanism.
body:
• The Bombay High Court said on October 15 that its ban on bursting firecrackers on public streets, lanes and footpaths applies throughout the year and to all festivals, not only Diwali.
  • The order extends a September 22 direction first issued during Ganeshotsav in a suo motu case on noise and air pollution in Maharashtra.
  • The court directed Maharashtra, the BMC and the state pollution board to issue public notices, run awareness campaigns within a week, promote green crackers and set up a complaint mechanism with police.
  • The court clarified it has not banned the manufacture or sale of firecrackers — the restriction covers bursting them in public places.

The Bombay High Court on Thursday extended its ban on bursting firecrackers on public streets, lanes and footpaths to every festival and every month of the year, weeks before Diwali, according to Bar and Bench.

A division bench of Justices Girish S. Kulkarni and Neela K. Gokhale said the September 22 order would remain in force year-round, covering Navratri, Diwali, Christmas and other celebrations. Reporting by the Press Trust of India, carried by News89, said the bench linked the direction to pollution that rises after Diwali and affects children and senior citizens in particular.

"The rights of citizens are paramount. The problem is the non-following of law."

— Bombay High Court bench, as reported by Bar and Bench

How the case began

The court took up the issue on its own motion in a public interest case concerning amplified sound and firecrackers on public roads during festivals. The September 22 order, passed during Ganeshotsav, imposed a complete ban on bursting firecrackers on public roads and also addressed laser and high-intensity lights in processions, decibel monitoring and action against equipment that breaches noise limits. Thursday's hearing was the next step in that same proceeding, and the bench used it to make the firecracker direction permanent in scope rather than festival-specific.

What authorities must now do

The bench directed the Maharashtra government, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation and the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board to jointly issue notices stating that bursting firecrackers in public places — streets, lanes and footpaths — is not permitted. It also ordered awareness work: public notices on the health effects of firecracker pollution, campaigns in schools and on public transport within a week, celebrity participation, promotion of low-emission green crackers, and an efficient complaint mechanism run with the police.

The distinction in the order is precise. Celebrations themselves are not banned, private manufacture and sale are not banned, and the court did not impose a blanket ban on possessing firecrackers. What is prohibited is bursting them in shared public space, where smoke, noise and debris affect passers-by, motorists and residents who did not choose to take part.

Why it matters beyond Mumbai

For families in Maharashtra planning Diwali, the practical change is location: community celebrations that previously spilled onto roads will need designated private or permitted spaces, and housing societies will face the same public-space rule on their approach roads. For the diaspora, the ruling is a useful reference point when explaining local Diwali plans at home — many US, Canadian and British cities impose similar public-space and time-window rules, and organisers of large community Diwali events abroad routinely work within permits that mirror this logic.

What happens next

Enforcement now rests with the BMC, the pollution board and Mumbai Police, who must publish the notices and stand up the complaint mechanism the court ordered. Previous police orders in Mumbai, issued after the September direction, ran for a defined festive window and warned of action under noise, environment and explosives law. Whether the year-round scope changes on-the-ground enforcement after Diwali will be the test at the next major festivals, including Christmas and New Year.
